subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage: Wednesday night. Anirban's notes. Jeevan sat through the whole stand-up with his eyes half-open, answering in single words. My first thought was "lazy," and then "burnt out." Both are labels, and I don't know either. At lunch he ate alone and looked flat. I stopped myself from telling the team he was checked out. Instead I sat down and said, "You seem a bit low on energy this week. No pressure, but how are you finding things?" He said he's been up with his baby daughter every night and is just running on empty. So not lazy. Not even sad, just tired. I offered to take one of his tickets tomorrow and he said he'd think about it. I'm glad I asked before I told anyone anything.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan running on empty?
qa.a: He had been up with his baby daughter every night.

qa.q: What was Anirban thinking while watching Jeevan through the stand-up?
qa.a: First "lazy" and then "burnt out," but Anirban realised they were labels that could not be confirmed.

qa.q: What could Anirban do next?
qa.a: Anirban can follow up on the offer to take a ticket and keep checking in kindly without telling others. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt about being asked?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved to be noticed kindly instead of judged, since he opened up about the sleepless nights.

grounding: A young professional sees a coworker looking flat and tired, and replaces labelling with kind curiosity.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage: At the government school in the kasba, the other teachers had started calling Amandeep "the ghost". For three weeks she'd drifted through the staffroom looking flat and tired, answering in a word or two, never joining the tea-time gossip. "Lazy," the PT teacher muttered. "She's lost interest." Yusuf wasn't sure. She still corrected every notebook, and her classes were quiet and orderly. Maybe she was just a private person. Maybe something was wrong. He didn't want to guess or label. One afternoon, when the staffroom emptied, he put a glass of nimbu pani on her desk. "You've looked tired lately. Totally fine if you don't want to say, but is there anything that would help?" She looked up, surprised. "I'm getting over typhoid. The doctor said I could come back, but I'm exhausted by noon." Yusuf nodded. "Want me to take your after-lunch playground duty for a couple of weeks?" "Yes," she said, and her face finally softened.

qa.q: What were the other teachers calling Amandeep?
qa.a: 'The ghost'.

qa.q: What did Yusuf think Amandeep's flatness might mean?
qa.a: Yusuf felt unsure and concerned, wondering whether she was simply private or something was wrong, and didn't want to label her.

qa.q: How did Yusuf show kind curiosity instead of labelling?
qa.a: He waited for a private moment, brought nimbu pani, gently named what he saw, gave her the option not to say, and offered practical help.

qa.q: How had the PT teacher read Amandeep?
qa.a: The PT teacher labelled her lazy and uninterested, missing that she was recovering from typhoid.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing a colleague's flat, tired manner and choosing kind curiosity over the label others gave her.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage: In the Edinburgh office, Freya had gone very quiet during the three-week audit. Her face was neutral all day, headphones on, her replies in the team chat reduced to "ok" and "done". Liam, who'd just read an article about burnout, started to worry. Should he tell their manager she was struggling? Instead he waited for the coffee break and asked, lightly, "You've been in deep-focus mode for weeks. Are you all right, or is it getting too much?" Freya pulled off one headphone and smiled. "I'm honestly fine. This is just what I look like when I'm concentrating. My family calls it my fish face." Liam laughed, relieved. "I nearly told Karen you were burnt out." "Please don't!" she said. "But thanks for asking me first. If I ever am, I'll tell you." She put the headphone back on and her face went neutral again, and this time Liam didn't read anything into it.

qa.q: How long was the audit?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling as Freya went quiet?
qa.a: Liam felt worried and concerned, having just read about burnout and wondering if she was struggling.

qa.q: Why was asking better than telling the manager Freya was burnt out?
qa.a: Asking revealed she was simply concentrating and fine, avoiding a wrong label and an unnecessary report to the manager.

qa.q: How does Freya see her neutral face during focus?
qa.a: Freya sees it as her normal concentration face, which her family calls her 'fish face', and appreciated being asked first.

grounding: Shows a young professional nearly labelling a colleague's neutral manner as burnout, and a kind question revealing it was focus.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage: On Ward 6 of the city hospital, patients' families had started saying Madhav was cold. He did everything right, but his face was flat, his voice neutral, and he no longer joked with the older patients the way he used to. One daughter complained at the desk that he didn't care. Reena, who had worked beside him for a year, didn't think that was it. She'd noticed him yawning through handovers and eating lunch standing up. At the end of the night shift, she caught him at the lockers. "You seem really worn down lately, and I miss your terrible jokes. How are you doing, honestly?" Madhav leaned against the locker. "I've done nine double shifts this month. We're short three nurses. I think I've got nothing left to give." Reena nodded. "That's not you being cold. That's you being empty. Can we go to Sister Philomena together tomorrow about the roster? And the staff counsellor is good." He managed a small smile. "Tomorrow."

qa.q: How many double shifts had Madhav done that month?
qa.a: Nine double shifts.

qa.q: What did Madhav say he was feeling?
qa.a: Madhav felt exhausted and depleted, saying he had nothing left to give after so many double shifts.

qa.q: How did Reena respond with kind curiosity rather than a label?
qa.a: She warmly named what she'd noticed, asked how he really was, reframed it as exhaustion rather than coldness, offered to go with him to the ward in-charge, and suggested the counsellor.

qa.q: How had the patients' families read Madhav's flat manner?
qa.a: They took it as coldness and not caring, with one daughter complaining that he didn't care.

grounding: Shows a young nurse noticing a colleague's flat, weary manner and asking kindly instead of accepting the label 'cold'.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage:
Subject: Checking in (no need to reply today)

Hi Neelam,

This is a slightly awkward email, so bear with me. For the last two weeks you've seemed quieter in stand-ups: short answers, camera off, no jokes about the office printer. On Tuesday I heard myself tell Rohit in the pantry that you were "totally burnt out." I had no business saying that, and I'm sorry. I don't actually know. You might be deep in the audit, unwell, dealing with something at home, or maybe this is just a heads-down season for you.

So instead of guessing, I'm asking: how are you doing? If you want to talk, I'm free for a walk at lunch any day this week. If you'd rather not, that's completely fine too, and I'll keep my pantry opinions to myself. 🙂

Take care,
Nirmala

qa.q: What did Nirmala tell Rohit in the pantry on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala said Neelam was "totally burnt out."

qa.q: Why did Nirmala write this email, and what was Nirmala feeling?
qa.a: Nirmala felt guilty about labelling Neelam to Rohit and concerned about the quiet stand-ups, while knowing the quietness might only mean a busy audit or a heads-down season.

qa.q: What could Nirmala have said to Rohit instead on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala could have said, "I don't know, I'll ask," and then checked in with Neelam directly rather than offering a label.

qa.q: What would it be like for Neelam to hear from Rohit that colleagues think Neelam is burnt out?
qa.a: Neelam might feel talked about and exposed, especially if the quiet was only focus on the audit, and could trust the team less.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional noticing a coworker's flat, quiet manner and choosing kind curiosity over a label.
